Hospital-Acquired Infections

What HAIs are, common types, risk factors and how to prevent them.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Define hospital-acquired infection
  • List common types of HAIs
  • Describe how to prevent HAIs

In simple words

Hospital-acquired infections (HAIs) are infections patients get while receiving care in a healthcare facility — they were not present or incubating at admission. They are also called nosocomial infections.

HAIs increase hospital stay, cost and risk of death. Nurses are frontline in preventing them through hand hygiene, asepsis and standard precautions.

Common types of HAIs

Type Common sites Common causes
CAUTI Urinary tract Catheters
CLABSI Bloodstream Central lines
VAP Lungs Ventilators
SSI Surgical wound Surgery
Pneumonia Lungs Bedrest, aspiration

Risk factors

  • Invasive devices (catheters, ventilators, central lines).
  • Surgery and wounds.
  • Weak immunity (elderly, babies, diabetes, cancer, steroids).
  • Long hospital stay.
  • Poor hand hygiene and asepsis.

Prevention

  • Hand hygiene before and after every patient contact.
  • Aseptic technique for all invasive procedures.
  • Remove catheters and lines as soon as no longer needed.
  • Clean and disinfect equipment between patients.
  • Standard precautions for every patient.

🔴 HAIs are preventable

Most HAIs are preventable with hand hygiene, aseptic technique and removing devices early. Every nurse’s responsibility.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Hand hygiene — the single most important HAI prevention measure.
  • Catheter care — assess daily if still needed; remove as soon as possible.
  • Ventilator care — head of bed up, oral care, suction asepsis.
  • Wound care — aseptic dressing changes; watch for redness, pus, fever.
  • Surveillance — report infection signs (fever, redness, purulent discharge) early.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. HAIs are infections acquired during healthcare, not present at admission.
  2. Common HAIs: CAUTI, CLABSI, VAP, SSI, pneumonia.
  3. Risk factors: invasive devices, surgery, weak immunity, long stay.
  4. Prevention: hand hygiene, aseptic technique, remove devices early.
  5. Standard precautions for every patient.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. CAUTI = catheter-associated urinary tract infection.
  2. CLABSI = central line-associated bloodstream infection.
  3. VAP = ventilator-associated pneumonia.
  4. SSI = surgical site infection.
  5. Invasive devices increase HAI risk — use only when needed.

📌 Memory trick

Common HAIs: “C-C-V-S-P” — CAUTI, CLABSI, VAP, SSI, Pneumonia.

60-second revision

  • HAI = infection acquired during healthcare, not at admission.
  • Types: CAUTI, CLABSI, VAP, SSI, pneumonia.
  • Risk: catheters, lines, surgery, weak immunity, long stay.
  • Prevent: hand hygiene, asepsis, remove devices early.
  • Report infection signs early.

Test yourself

An HAI is an infection:

Answer: B. An HAI is acquired during healthcare delivery and was not present at admission.

CAUTI affects the:

Answer: C. CAUTI = catheter-associated urinary tract infection.

The single most important HAI prevention measure is:

Answer: B. Hand hygiene is the single most important measure to prevent HAI spread.

CLABSI is associated with:

Answer: B. CLABSI = central line-associated bloodstream infection.

Devices should be removed:

Answer: B. Remove invasive devices as soon as they are no longer needed to reduce infection risk.
